name: Color Carousel

card.note: the width of the card in front; its height follows from ratio

ratio.note: the card's width : height. 1 is the square the reference uses; 1.78 for a 16:9 screenshot.

spread.note: how far apart the cards sit, as a fraction of the card's width. The side cards are already narrower for having receded, so a shade over 1 is what opens a visible gap between them; below 1 they tuck behind each other.

depth.note: how far each step back recedes. With perspective, this is what shrinks the side cards - they are not separately scaled. perspective / (perspective + depth) is the shrink: the default pair gives the reference's three-quarters.

angle.note: how far a card off centre turns. A right-hand card turns its inner edge away, so the ring is seen from outside rather than from within.

perspective.note: the camera distance. Smaller is a wider lens and a more dramatic ring; much below 700 the far cards start to smear.

radius.note: the corner radius - the hub's tile radius, and the stage takes it too

reach.note: how many cards each side stay on the stage. The last one is mid-fade, so three shows two clearly.

wash.note: how much of the card's colour reaches the stage in the light theme

glow.note: the same in the dark theme, where a colour on a dark ground has to work much harder to be seen at all

saturate.note: the sampled colour is pushed this far toward full chroma. 1 uses the picture's own colour, which is usually too soft to light a stage with.

dwell.note: how long a card holds the front before the next one. A loop length, so it is an option rather than a token.

step.note: how long the arrow takes to walk to the next card before pressing it

interactive.note: drag, wheel-free arrow keys, and click a card to bring it forward

autoplay.note: advance on its own when no pointer is on the stage

cursor.note: mount the library's User Cursor on the stage. Off, the carousel answers the real pointer only.

name.note: the cursor's pill. Empty here on purpose - the cards are the thing to look at, and a name floating over a photograph is one label too many.

accent.note: passed to the cursor. auto follows --navy: Tech Blue on a light ground, Innovation Blue on a dark one.

paused.note: stops the tour and the arrow together - pausing one without the other leaves a cursor pressing cards that never come forward

compact.note: the card-sized skin, for a stage under ~200px

reducedMotion: The carousel still works - it is a control, not decoration. What goes is the self-driving tour, the glide between cards and the colour's cross-fade: a card arrives in front instead of travelling there, and the stage changes colour instead of bleeding into the next one. Drag, arrow keys and clicking a card are untouched.
notPorted: the gradient itself. The reference reads a gradient definition off each slide and paints the background with it; this one samples the card's own pixels, which is the whole difference - drop photographs in and the light follows them with nobody picking colours.
colour as a free value. accent is one of four palette names, or auto, and anything else throws. The sampled wash is exempt: it comes from the picture, which is the point.
a spring on the ring. The glide is exponential smoothing on one time constant, because that is what the rest of this library uses.
slides as React nodes. A card is any direct child element, moved across whole - so the markup stays a plain list of images with this module removed.
brandNotes: Not a port. The source is React Bits Pro: the code is behind a subscription and its licence (§2.4) forbids putting the source in a repository or making it available to third parties - this repo is public and ships a reusable bundle in dist/, which is exactly the case that clause names. So the motion idea was rebuilt from the documented behaviour and a screen recording, on the Continia tokens, and it was rebuilt differently on purpose: the reference is a gradient carousel and this is a colour carousel, taking its light from the card's own pixels rather than from a gradient someone wrote down. The sampler bins pixels into a coarse 6x6x6 cube and drops the near-white, near-black and near-grey ones before averaging the biggest bucket, because a flat mean of a green field under a blue sky is grey. Palette discipline is unchanged where the module chooses a colour - the demo tiles are Tech Blue, Smart Green, Performance Purple and Innovation Blue, and the cursor's accent is still one of four names - but the wash is sampled, not chosen, so a photograph lights the stage in its own colour. The arrow is the library's own User Cursor, mounted rather than redrawn, and here with an empty name so the pill stays out of the way; that module gained the empty-name case for this.
blurb: A 3D carousel whose stage lights up in the colour of the card in front. Made for photographs: the colour is read off the picture's own pixels, so a green shot washes the stage green and the next one warms it, with nobody picking a palette to match.

name: Hover Preview

width.note: the preview card; its height follows from ratio

ratio.note: the card's width : height. 1 is the square the reference uses; 1.78 for a 16:9 screenshot.

gap.note: between the bottom edge of the card and the top of the word

tilt.note: the widest resting angle, either way. Each word's angle is derived from its key rather than drawn at random, so a card leans the same way on every load - a word that flips sides on reload reads as a bug, not as a hand-placed card. Set data-hp-tilt on a trigger to pin one.

parallax.note: how far the card slides as the cursor crosses the word, so it leans toward the side being read instead of sitting dead centre

follow.note: a time constant, not a transition: the card closes 63% of the gap to the word it is heading for in this long. Off the duration scale (--motion-duration-moderate), one step above the arrow's own follow - the card is the heavier object and should arrive after the cursor does.

dwell.note: how long the self-driving tour rests on each word before moving to the next. A loop length, so it is an option rather than a token.

cursor.note: mount the library's User Cursor on the stage. Off, the preview answers the real pointer only and the page keeps its own cursor.

accent.note: passed to the cursor. auto follows --navy: Tech Blue on a light ground, Innovation Blue on a dark one.

autoplay.note: tour the words when no pointer is on the stage

paused.note: stops the tour and the glide together - pausing one without the other leaves a cursor touring words whose preview never opens

compact.note: the card-sized skin - smaller copy, card and type, for a stage under ~200px

reducedMotion: No tour, no glide, no lean. The words still work and the card still appears on hover - it appears where it belongs, at rest, and the lift and the cross-fade stop animating. The self-driving demo is the part that goes: a card that moves on its own is exactly what the setting is asking not to happen.
notPorted: colour as a free value - the source takes any hex. Here accent is one of four palette names, or auto, and anything else throws.
the preview as a React node passed per item. A trigger's card comes from a <template data-hp-for>, from data-hp-img, or from the trigger's own text - the same three sources, without a component tree.

follow-the-pointer positioning. The reference anchors the card to the word and lets the pointer nudge it; measured off the recording, the card travels exactly the distance between two word centres and wobbles about 4px while a word is held. That is an anchor with parallax, not a follower, and it is what is built here.
a spring. The glide is exponential smoothing on one time constant, because that is what the rest of this library uses and a second motion model for one card is not worth the surface.
brandNotes: Not a port. The source is React Bits Pro: the code is behind a subscription and its licence (§2.4) forbids putting the source in a repository or making it available to third parties - this repo is public and ships a reusable bundle in dist/, which is exactly the case that clause names. So the motion idea was rebuilt from the documented behaviour and a screen recording, on the Continia tokens. sourceUrl points at the page that describes the idea, for provenance, not at code that was copied. Timings were measured off the recording rather than guessed: the card lifts from 74% over about 250ms, the handoff between two words glides and cross-fades over about 360ms instead of closing and reopening, and each card rests at a small angle of its own rather than hanging straight. The arrow is the library's own User Cursor, mounted rather than redrawn, so the two entries cannot drift apart; that module gained two hooks for this - autoPath, which replaces its wander with a tour of the words, and at(), which reports where its tip is heading. Hit-testing reads at() rather than the real pointer, so the preview and the arrow can never disagree about which word is hovered, including while the cursor is driving itself.
blurb: A paragraph whose key words are live: put the cursor on one and a small card lifts above it. Move to the next and the same card glides across and cross-fades rather than closing and reopening, so the reader's eye never has to find it again.

name: Magic Transform

docCount.note: procedural documents in rotation; [data-mt-doc] children override them

docDuration.note: travel time to the axis - a loop length, not a transition, so an option rather than a token

resultCount.note: distinct pieces in rotation; [data-mt-result] children override them

resultsPerBeat.note: pieces thrown each time a document goes under the axis; each gets its own lane, so they never stack

resultLife.note: the longest a thrown piece may live. It is also capped at 92% of the beat, so a burst is always gone before the next document goes under - a loop length, so an option rather than a token

resultSpread.note: 0-1, how much of the free space to the right the fan reaches into

maxResults.note: live pieces before the oldest is dropped; a floor under a backlog, not the usual limit - pieces expire on their own

compact.note: the card-sized skin - thinner bars and smaller pieces, for a stage under ~200px

seed.note: deterministic texture and fan, so a reload looks the same

reducedMotion: Nothing travels and nothing bursts. The stage lays out a static frame instead - one document parked short of the axis, the axis lit, and the pieces already spread across the far side - so the picture still says what the machine does.
notPorted: axisColor - the default is #7C3AED, which is off the Continia palette. The axis takes var(--navy) instead, so it is Tech Blue in light mode and Innovation Blue in dark without a second value to keep in sync.
backgroundColor - the stage is transparent and sits on whatever surface hosts it; a page that needs a ground sets it on the wrapper.
width - CSS's job. The element is display:block and fills its container; only height is an option because the stage has to know its own.
centerContent as a ReactNode - there is no React here, so the core takes a [data-mt-core] child. With none, it draws the quarter circle from the logomark.
classNames / className / style - a vanilla caller styles the element and the documented classes directly.
documents / results as data arrays - passed as [data-mt-doc] and [data-mt-result] template children instead, which keeps the markup copyable without a build step.
brandNotes: Not a port. The source is React Bits Pro: the code is behind a subscription and its licence (§2.4) forbids putting the source in a repository or making it available to third parties - this repo is public and ships a reusable bundle in dist/, which is exactly the case that clause names. So the motion idea was rebuilt from the documented behaviour, on the Continia tokens. sourceUrl points at the page that describes the idea, for provenance, not at code that was copied. Two brand corrections against the reference: the axis is not the source's purple #7C3AED but var(--navy), and the confetti and the chips on the thrown pieces use the four brand colours only - Tech Blue, Innovation Blue, Smart Green and Performance Purple - where the reference fans out an open palette. The core tile takes --navy, so it is Tech Blue on a light ground and Innovation Blue on a dark one, and the mark on it is always the opposite - white on the Tech Blue tile, Tech Blue on the cyan one. The hourglass ships as one white SVG and is painted as a mask over the tile's ink rather than kept as a second, recoloured file; the logomark itself is still only ever White or Tech Blue, which is exactly the two values this produces.

Measured off the recording the open card is 3.2x wider but only 1.9x taller than its slot, so a plain scale would turn the 15px radius into an ellipse and arrive with the body text stretched. The morph is a FLIP instead, and the title grows on font-size - a property, not a transform - so it stays crisp the whole way.

the card list as React children with per-card props. A card is any direct child element and the module reads it: first image is the media, first heading the title, first paragraph the body. The source stays a readable list of articles with the module removed.

damping.note: per frame at 60fps, rescaled for other refresh rates

name: User Cursor

name.note: what the pill trailing the arrow says. Empty hides the pill: the arrow on its own, for a stage where a name would be one thing too many.

accent.note: auto | blue | cyan | green | purple. Palette only - an unknown value throws rather than painting an off-brand cursor. auto follows --navy, so Tech Blue on a light ground and Innovation Blue on a dark one.

size.note: the arrow's width; the pill's offset and type scale off it. The arrow is a three-pointed concave arrowhead, not the OS pointer with its rectangular tail.

follow.note: a time constant, not a transition: the arrow closes 63% of the gap to the pointer in this long, so a bigger number is a softer, later cursor. Off the duration scale (--motion-duration-fast). It cannot go much higher without the arrow leaving the stage on a fast move - a lagging follower sits speed x this far behind whatever it chases.

labelFollow.note: the same for the pill, one step up the scale (--motion-duration-base). The difference between the two is the only thing that makes the pill trail - there is no hardcoded offset.

maxTrail.note: the furthest the pill may fall behind the arrow. The trail grows with speed and would leave the stage unbounded, so the pill is pulled back onto a leash rather than given a shorter lag - a slow move still reads as a soft follow.

tilt.note: the most the arrow may lean into a move; it reaches this at 1.6px/ms of the ARROW's own speed and no further, so a fast flick cannot spin it. The angle is eased on --motion-duration-instant and the speed is read raw, because the arrow's position is already smoothed - stacking more lag on top and the lean never arrives on a short move.

drift.note: one wander cycle with no pointer on the stage - a loop length, so an option rather than a token

autoplay.note: wander when no pointer is present. false makes it an ordinary custom cursor: hidden until the pointer enters.

hideNative.note: hide the real cursor, and only while the pointer is inside the stage

compact.note: the card-sized skin - smaller arrow, pill and demo type, for a stage under ~200px

autoPath.note: (clock, W, H) -> [x, y], replacing the sine wander. The point it returns is where the arrow's TIP should go, not where its box starts, so a caller aiming at a word does not have to know the arrow's geometry. Read it back with at(), which reports the tip's target and which source is setting it - a component built on this one hit-tests against that rather than against the real pointer, so the two can never disagree about what is hovered. Hover Preview is what these two exist for. A function, so init/update only - never a data- attribute.

reducedMotion: No loop and no wander. The cursor is still there and still follows the pointer, but it is written straight through with no smoothing and no lean, so there is never a moving element nobody asked for - and never an invisible pointer either, which is the trap with a custom cursor.
notPorted: colour as a free value - the source takes any hex. Here accent is one of four palette names, or auto, and anything else throws. An off-palette cursor is the exact failure the brand rule exists to stop.
multiple remote cursors driven by a presence backend - there is no socket here. One cursor, driven by the pointer or by its own wander.
className / style props - a vanilla caller styles .mluc, .mluc-cur and .mluc-pill directly.
width - CSS's job. The element is display:block and fills its container; only height is an option, because the stage has to know its own.

brandNotes: Not a port. The source is React Bits Pro: the code is behind a subscription and its licence (§2.4) forbids putting the source in a repository or making it available to third parties - this repo is public and ships a reusable bundle in dist/, which is exactly the case that clause names. So the motion idea was rebuilt from the documented behaviour and a screen recording, on the Continia tokens. sourceUrl points at the page that describes the idea, for provenance, not at code that was copied. The silhouette is traced 1:1 off the reference - a three-pointed concave arrowhead rather than the OS arrow, measured at the two frames where it is standing still so its own lean is not baked into the shape. The finish comes from a second reference: all three points rounded to one viewBox unit (5% of an edge, measured off corner arcs of 17-20px on a 340px render), a fill that is one colour at a falling alpha rather than flat paint, a slightly brighter rim on the same ramp, and a soft glow offset down-right - the reference's soft band is ~1% of the arrow on the top-left edge and four times that on the bottom right, which is a light from the upper left rather than an even halo. Fill, rim and glow all read the one accent, so nothing can drift off the palette and light mode stays Tech Blue. Two deliberate differences from the reference: the reference cursor is orange, which is not a Continia colour, so the default follows --navy and the pill's text takes the opposite value - white on the Tech Blue arrow in light mode, Tech Blue on the Innovation Blue one in dark - and the motion is slower than the reference on request, with both time constants taken off the duration scale, the lean damped on --motion-duration-fast so a fast move eases the arrow over rather than snapping it, and the pill's trail put on a 56px leash so speed can never fling it off the stage.
blurb: A second cursor on the stage: a rounded, glass-tinted arrowhead that leans into the direction it is travelling, with a name pill trailing a step behind it. It follows the pointer when there is one and wanders on its own when there is not.
